episode_title: Could Your Biggest Sales Breakthrough Have Nothing to Do With Selling?

real_qa.q: How does Corey Charles help salespeople overcome rejection and fear of saying no in sales?
real_qa.r: Charles teaches salespeople to divorce themselves from the outcome by understanding that a no from a prospect is not personal rejection. He explains that prospects are saying no to the situation, not to the salesman as a human being. Once salespeople stop viewing rejection as personal and instead see it as feedback about fit or timing, asking for the sale becomes less intimidating. He also coaches teams to recognize physical tells when they are not at their best mentally and to develop reset mechanisms like calling a friend, listening to music, or taking a walk to quickly reboot before engaging the next prospect.
real_qa.requete: how to overcome rejection fear in sales

real_qa.q: What is Corey Charles's approach to mindset as the foundation for sales success?
real_qa.r: Charles emphasizes that mindset is more important than techniques or scripts. He states if you get your mind right, you get your money right. He explains that strategy and sales skills mean nothing if the thoughts between your ears are not aligned, and that 80% of conversations with sales teams focus on fixing mindset rather than adding more techniques. He illustrates this by noting that new salespeople often perform well because they are not bogged down by baggage and rejections accumulated over time, and advises that if salespeople cannot achieve complete control of mindset, they should at least maintain excitement and positive energy, as people respond to energy.

real_qa.q: Why does Corey Charles believe new salespeople are more successful than experienced ones?
real_qa.r: Charles explains that new salespeople show up and start selling successfully because they are not weighed down by all the baggage, rejections, and accumulated nos that happen to salespeople over time. New salespeople are simply excited about life and excited about the opportunity, which translates into genuine enthusiasm that prospects respond to. He contrasts this with veteran salespeople who may carry emotional weight from past rejections.

real_qa.q: What reset mechanisms does Corey Charles recommend for salespeople after rejection?
real_qa.r: Charles advises salespeople to identify their personal physical tells that indicate they are not at their best mentally, such as body getting hot or eyebrows feeling heavy. Once they recognize these signals, he recommends having firewalls in place to reset and reboot, whether through calling a friend, listening to music, taking a walk, or reading a book. The goal is to ensure the next prospect encounters the salesperson at full mental capacity and not at 90% because of carrying a previous no.

real_qa.q: How did Corey Charles develop his obsession with learning and studying successful salespeople?
real_qa.r: Charles attributes his drive to learn to both natural curiosity instilled from childhood and encouragement from his mother, who always taught him that curiosity is a good thing. His mother respected his questions and taught him to be curious in order to learn something new rather than out of idle interest. This mindset led him to study great performers, take notes, read books, and become a monster for knowledge in pursuit of mastering sales skills. He learned that success leaves clues and made it his job to pick up those breadcrumbs from top performers.
real_qa.requete: learning from great salespeople study mindset

guest.bio_context: Corey Charles grew up in Brooklyn, New York, and later moved to Orlando, Florida. He initially pursued graphic design but fell into a sales role by accident, eventually becoming skilled at sales through studying great performers and reading extensively. He transitioned from sales into roles as a sales trainer and leadership coach, where he discovered that approximately 80% of his conversations centered on mindset. He has also worked across multiple sales verticals including automotive and new home sales, and recently released a book addressing how past stories shape current mindset.
